newsitem.title: USA: Airline stocks hit by fears of higher taxes.
newsitem.headline: Airline stocks hit by fears of higher taxes.

text.p: Airline stocks slid Thursday on fears that tax proposals emerging from Congress would bite into the industry's profits, analysts said.
Airline stocks were initially hit after investment bank Goldman Sachs downgraded its investment ratings on the nation's three largest airlines, citing concerns about the tax proposals.

"The government is telling you that to pay for the middle-class tax cut and the capital gains tax cut, it means screwing the airlines, in particular the international airlines," said Goldman Sachs airline analyst Glenn Engel.
Goldman downgraded AMR Corp., UAL Corp. and Delta Air Lines Inc., sparking a selloff in other airline stocks, analysts and traders said.

By midday, the American Stock Exchange airline index shed almost nine points, or 1.9 percent, to 460 and the Dow Jones transportation average fell almost 19 points, or 0.69 percent, to 2,719. AMR fell $1.25 to $94, Delta lost $1.375 to $87.875 and UAL was down $1.375 to $72.875, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
In the past two weeks, the U.S. Senate Finance Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee have proposed conflicting plans that would increase taxes on the airline industry.
"Two distinct proposals have emerged. The only thing they have in common is that they would raise taxes for the industry," said Samuel Buttrick, an airline analyst with PaineWebber Group Inc.

"The House version was bad. But the Senate proposal is even worse than the House ... Before I thought the tax was a threat, but a threat that could possibly be minimised. But after the Senate proposal, I just feel that it is no longer a threat that can be dismissed," Engel said.
To offset the higher taxes, airlines could try to boost fares on international flights. But the new taxes would eat into profits the airlines would normally keep for themselves.
"Whatever you thought profits were going to be, the government would now take some of that," Engel said.

Engel estimates the House proposal would increase the industry's taxes to $31 billion over five years, while the Senate version would boost taxes to $33 billion over the same period. The current tax burden for the U.S. airline industry is about $25 billion over five years, Engel said.
Other analysts said concerns about the tax proposals are premature, since the proposals will probably change significantly before a final tax plan is enacted.
Airlines have lobbied fiercly against the tax proposals.

Smaller airlines, such as Southwest Airlines Co., object strongly to the House proposal, which would introduce a per passenger "head tax" on domestic flights. Small carriers said the flat, per person tax, would impose an unfair burden on regional carriers and consumers who are less able to afford price increases.
Southwest and some regional airlines started a national advertising campaign this week called "Skyway Robbery," which urges consumers to say "No" to the proposed head tax.
Larger carriers in the so-called Coalition for Fair FAA Funding have also spoken out against the Senate proposal.

The coalition said the Senate proposal will hit consumers travelling internationally the hardest. The group estimates the tax increase would force an estimated 1 million travelers a year to drop international travel plans.
"This proposal translates to a complete and total depression of the travel and tourism industry," Will Ris, vice president of government affairs for AMR's American Airlines, said in a statement.
"Neither the industry nor the consumer should be forced to take on the burden of balancing the budget by paying an additional $8 billion in taxes on airline taxes over the next five years," Ris said.

The House and Senate proposals offer an alternative to the current 10 percent passenger excise tax on domestic travel. The tax, which is expected to expire in September, funds the Federal Aviation Administration.

The House proposal would impose an international arrival and departure fee of $15.50 per passenger, up from the current $6 fee. The proposal would also reduce the 10 percent excise tax on domestic travel to 7.5 percent, but introduce a domestic per passenger "head" tax, analysts said.

The Senate version would extend the airline ticket tax but would reduce the air passenger ticket tax rate to 7.5 percent from 10 percent for flights in certain rural areas. The bill would repeal the $6 international departure tax and impose a 10 percent tax on the part of the international ticket price attributable to the portion of the flight in U.S. airspace.
